notes: Alan Cohen is a real inspirational author (The Dragon Doesn't Live Here Anymore, A Deep Breath of Life, Wisdom of the Heart) and this line circulates consistently under his name on quote sites and in daily-inspiration compilations. I cannot place it in a specific book, chapter, or dated column from training knowledge, and Cohen's aphorisms are almost always recirculated without citation. The attribution is plausible and uncontested but unsourced.

Consistently attributed to Gandhi across collections, and the ocean/drops image is idiomatically consistent with his writing in Young India and Harijan. However, I cannot locate a primary source — no specific issue, speech, or volume of the Collected Works comes to mind, and I do not know whether this sits in the sourced or the unsourced section of Gandhi's Wikiquote page. Gandhi is a heavy misattribution magnet, so consistent repetition is not itself evidence. Honest verdict: plausibly genuine, unverified.

The pre-flag is correct. There is no Gandhi source for this; it does not appear in the Collected Works so far as I know, and it is generally listed among Gandhi's misattributed lines. The saying is far older than Gandhi: a closely matching maxim ('Study as if you were to live forever; live as if you were to die tomorrow') is traditionally ascribed to St. Edmund of Abingdon, the 13th-century Archbishop of Canterbury, and circulated in English proverb collections well before Gandhi's lifetime. The James Dean attribution is a separate later graft and is also unsupported. I am confident it is not Gandhi's; I am only moderately confident in the Edmund of Abingdon lineage, which is itself a tradition rather than a documented autograph.
suggested_reattribution: Traditional maxim long ascribed to St. Edmund of Abingdon (13th c.); not Gandhi

earliest_print_source: Statement to Christian Zervos, 'Conversation avec Picasso,' Cahiers d'Art, 1935
notes: This belongs to Picasso's well-known 1935 statement recorded by Christian Zervos and published in Cahiers d'Art, the same conversation that produced 'a picture is not thought out and settled beforehand.' The English rendering circulating today comes from the translation reprinted in Alfred H. Barr Jr.'s Picasso monograph and in Herschel B. Chipp's Theories of Modern Art (1968). I am confident about the 1935 Zervos conversation as the origin but have not pinned the exact page in the translated reprints, so I am holding just under the promotion bar rather than claiming primary verification.

Idiomatically very close to Watts's recurring theme that naming and classifying substitute for direct perception (developed at length in The Wisdom of Insecurity and The Book), but I cannot place this exact sentence in any Watts book or transcribed lecture. Watts's recorded talks are a large, loosely transcribed corpus, which makes attractive one-liners easy to attach to him without evidence. Plausible but unsourced.

The thought is authentically Jungian — it matches his insistence that the psyche is not contained inside the skull ('we are in the psyche' rather than the psyche being in us) and his late work on synchronicity and the unus mundus. But I cannot locate this exact sentence in the Collected Works, the letters, or Memories, Dreams, Reflections. Jung is frequently paraphrased into crisper English than he wrote, and this reads like such a condensation. Unsourced.

earliest_print_source: 'The Most Durable Power,' Martin Luther King Jr., The Christian Century, 1957 (from a sermon delivered at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, Montgomery, November 1956)
notes: This is King's own language from the sermon/essay 'The Most Durable Power,' delivered at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church during the closing weeks of the Montgomery bus boycott and excerpted in The Christian Century in 1957; it is indexed in The Papers of Martin Luther King, Jr. and reprinted in A Testament of Hope. The wording here (durable power / creative force / exemplified in the life of our Christ / quest for peace and security) matches the published text. I am confident in the sermon and the Christian Century publication; I am not certain of the exact issue date, so treat the year rather than a day as the firm part of the citation.

earliest_print_source: 'What I Believe,' Albert Einstein, Forum and Century, vol. 84, 1930; collected in The World As I See It, 1931 (Mein Weltbild, 1934)
notes: Genuine Einstein, and unusually well documented for him. This is the closing passage of his credo essay 'What I Believe,' published in Forum and Century in 1930 and collected in The World As I See It. The long form quoted here matches the standard English translation, including 'as good as dead; his eyes are closed' and the concluding 'this knowledge, this feeling is at the center of true religiousness.' Truncated one-line versions circulate widely, but the full passage given here is faithful.

The pre-flag is correct. There is no Einstein source for this, in his published papers, essays, letters, or the standard quotation references. It reads as a design-industry aphorism of recent vintage, most likely a loose descendant of the genuine Einstein simplicity theme (see q_0180) that acquired his name for authority. I cannot identify a real originator, so 'apocryphal' rather than 'likely_misattributed' — I have no probable true author to offer, and inventing one would be worse than admitting that.

earliest_print_source: Roger Sessions, 'How a Difficult Composer Gets That Way,' The New York Times, January 8, 1950
notes: The idea is Einstein's; the epigram is not his wording. Einstein's documented statement is from the 1933 Herbert Spencer Lecture 'On the Method of Theoretical Physics': the supreme goal of all theory is to make the irreducible basic elements as simple and as few as possible without surrendering the adequate representation of a single datum of experience. The compact form entered print when the composer Roger Sessions reported it secondhand in the New York Times in 1950 — explicitly as a remark Einstein made 'in effect,' i.e. Sessions's own condensation. Everything since descends from that paraphrase. Genuine sentiment, secondhand phrasing; deliberately held below the promotion bar because the corpus would be presenting a paraphrase as Einstein's words.

earliest_print_source: Richard L. Evans's Quote Book, 1971 (crediting Carl W. Buehner)
notes: The pre-flag is right to hedge. Angelou did use versions of this in interviews and talks from the 1990s onward, so the attribution is not fabricated — but the aphorism predates her. The earliest known instance credits Carl W. Buehner: 'They may forget what you said, but they will never forget how you made them feel,' printed in Richard L. Evans's Quote Book (1971). Angelou's characteristic triad ('what you said / what you did / how you made them feel') is her expansion of an existing saying, and I cannot fix a first Angelou utterance or its exact wording. Safest handling: treat the wording as unverified and do not present it as an original Angelou line.

Definitely not Lincoln — nothing like it appears in the Collected Works, and the managerial idiom is anachronistic for the 1860s; it is a standard Lincoln graft. The Drucker attribution in the author field is the common replacement but is itself weakly evidenced: I cannot point to the book or article where Drucker wrote it. The best-documented neighbor is Alan Kay's 'The best way to predict the future is to invent it' (Xerox PARC, early 1970s), and Dennis Gabor's Inventing the Future (1963) argues that the future cannot be predicted but can be invented. The 'create it' variant floats between Drucker, Kay, Gabor, and Forrest Shaklee. Since I cannot say which is right, no reattribution.

Consistently and, as far as I know, uncontestedly attributed to the American essayist Agnes Repplier (1855-1950), and the epigrammatic balance is characteristic of her prose. It is usually cited to one of her essay collections — Compromises (1904) is the volume most often named — but I cannot confirm the volume or essay from memory, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing. Attribution is stable; the citation is not established.

Same situation as q_0166. Attributed to Alan Cohen wherever it appears and consistent with his register, but recirculated without citation and not placeable in a specific book or column from training knowledge. Uncontested but unsourced.

As with the other two Alan Cohen entries in this batch: plausible, uncontested, and unsourced. I cannot place it in a titled work, and Cohen's material circulates chiefly through daily-inspiration excerpts that drop citations.

Strongly Wattsian in both idea and vocabulary — 'aperture' is a word he genuinely used for the individual as the universe's point of self-awareness, and the thought parallels the documented passages in The Book: On the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are (1966) about the universe peopling and looking at itself through our eyes. I cannot confirm this exact sentence in a printed Watts text, and much of the Watts material online comes from loosely transcribed lectures. Likely genuine in substance, wording unverified.

One of the most widely reproduced Watts lines, attributed to him with unusual consistency and squarely on the theme of The Wisdom of Insecurity (1951), which is the book most often cited for it. I cannot confirm the page or even the volume from memory, so I am not recording a print source. The stability of the attribution earns 'attributed,' but without a located passage it stays below the promotion bar.

No primary source. This is one of the modest-genius lines that accrete to Einstein, and I cannot trace it to a paper, letter, or documented interview. The genuine, well-sourced neighbor is his letter to Carl Seelig of 11 March 1952: 'I have no special talents. I am only passionately curious.' The 'stay with problems longer' phrasing looks like a later restatement of that sentiment rather than something Einstein wrote. Uncertain, and Einstein's misattribution record argues for caution.

No Einstein source exists for this; it is routinely listed among his misattributed quotations. The phrasing is late-20th/21st-century motivational English and has the shape of a slogan retrofitted with a famous name — it may owe something to popularized readings of adaptability in intelligence research, but I know of no real originator and will not guess one. Recommend it not be promoted under Einstein's name in any form.

earliest_print_source: A Course in Miracles, Text, Chapter 21, Introduction (T-21.in.1), Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976
notes: Genuine and locatable. This is the opening of Chapter 21 of the ACIM Text ('Reason and Perception'), which begins 'Projection makes perception' and continues through 'Therefore, seek not to change the world, but choose to change your mind about the world.' The second sentence quoted here ('What you see reflects your thinking...') is from the same introductory passage. Wording matches the Foundation for Inner Peace edition. Note the source is a work, not a person — the corpus should credit A Course in Miracles rather than Helen Schucman personally, which matches the input.

The sentence matches ACIM's definition of the ego as the mind's belief in its own separation and autonomy, and it is quoted as ACIM in the secondary literature around the Course (Wapnick and others). I cannot pin the chapter and section, and ACIM circulates in multiple editions with different numbering, so I am not recording a citation I cannot place. Very likely genuine to the work; location unconfirmed.

Reads as authentic ACIM in cadence and doctrine (freedom of belief, and behavior as the witness to belief), and it is quoted as such, but I cannot locate the passage in the Text, Workbook, or Manual for Teachers from memory. Slightly lower confidence than q_0191 because I have less independent recall of this specific line. Genuine-looking but unlocated.

Extremely widely attributed to Helen Keller and not, to my knowledge, contested or reassigned to anyone else — but I cannot trace it to a book, essay, letter, or speech of hers. It is a staple of teamwork posters and fundraising copy, which is exactly the environment in which citations disappear. Plausible; unsourced.

Not Lincoln. Nothing of the kind appears in the Collected Works, and the attribution is 20th-century. The near-certain origin is Robert G. Ingersoll's celebrated lecture on Lincoln (1883), which argues: 'Nothing discloses real character like the use of power... Most people can bear adversity; but if you wish to know what a man really is, give him power.' A statement made *about* Lincoln was over time converted into a statement *by* Lincoln — a common mechanism for this particular magnet. Confidence value reflects the weakness of the Lincoln attribution; my confidence in the Ingersoll origin is considerably higher.
suggested_reattribution: Robert G. Ingersoll, from his 1883 lecture on Abraham Lincoln

earliest_print_source: Toward a Psychology of Being, Abraham H. Maslow, 1962
notes: The thought is documented Maslow: Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) frames growth as a repeated choice, in the form 'one can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth,' with growth chosen over and over and fear overcome again and again. The wording quoted here ('You will either step forward in growth or you will step back into safety') is the popular circulating variant rather than the printed sentence I can attest to, and it is often given in the second person as if from a lecture. Substance verified in the 1962 book; exact wording is a variant, so it should be presented as Maslow's idea, ideally with the printed phrasing substituted.
